L0@P0: Demand-Driven Risk Premia
L1@P0: in FX and Bond Markets
L2@P0: Ingomar Krohn∗ Andreas Uthemann† Rishi Vala‡ Jun Yang§
L3@P0: Abstract
L4@P0: We use high-frequency price changes around U.S. Treasury auctions to identify shifts in demand for U.S. safe assets and analyze their effects on foreign exchange and bond markets. A
L5@P0: positive demand shock for U.S. Treasuries leads, on average, to a 2-basis-point depreciation
L6@P0: of the U.S. dollar against a portfolio of G9 currencies, with the price impact increasing with
L7@P0: the maturity of the issued security. Countries with highly correlated short-term interest rates
L8@P0: to the U.S. experience weaker currency appreciation but stronger bond yield co-movement
L9@P0: with U.S. Treasuries, compared to countries with lower short-rate correlations. These findings provide robust support for segmented markets models, where global arbitrageurs act as
L10@P0: marginal investors in both foreign exchange and bond markets, and highlight the critical role
L11@P0: of risk premia in driving the co-movement of exchange rates and bond yields.
L12@P0: Keywords: Foreign exchange markets, risk premia, Treasury auctions, safe asset demand
L13@P0: JEL codes: F30, F31, G12, G15
L14@P0: This Version: January 2025.
L15@P0: We thank seminar participants at the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Bank of Canada. The views expressed in this
L16@P0: paper are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the position of the Bank of Canada. All errors are our
L17@P0: own.
L18@P0: ∗Corresponding Author. Bank of Canada, 234 Wellington St. W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0G9, Canada, Email:
L19@P0: IKrohn@bank-banque-canada.ca
L20@P0: †Bank of Canada, 234 Wellington St. W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0G9, Canada, Email: AUthemann@bank-banque-canada.ca
L21@P0: ‡Bank of Canada, 234 Wellington St. W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0G9, Canada, Email: RVala@bank-banque-canada.ca
L22@P0-1: §Bank of Canada, 234 Wellington St. W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0G9, Canada, Email: JYang@bank-banque-canada.caI. Introduction
L23@P1: The co-movement of exchange rates and bond yields is conceptually well understood, as both are
L24@P1: strongly influenced by changes in short-term interest rates. Building on this shared interest-rate
L25@P1: sensitivity, recent work by Gourinchas et al. (2022) and Greenwood et al. (2023) develops a
L26@P1: theoretical framework that links risk premia in exchange rate and bond markets. Their work
L27@P1: provides clear predictions regarding the strength and direction of the co-movement between bond
L28@P1: yields and exchange rates in response to shifts in investors’ demand for bonds. Central to the
L29@P1: approach are global arbitrageurs, who absorb demand shocks from preferred-habitat investors in
L30@P1: domestic and foreign bond markets as well as in foreign exchange (FX) markets. As marginal
L31@P1: investors, these arbitrageurs play a pivotal role in setting the price of risk across all three markets,
L32@P1: with variations in risk premia arising from changes in their portfolios
L33@P1: The tight link across these markets implies that shifts in the demand for U.S. government
L34@P1: bonds can generate significant spillover effects into both global bond yields and exchange rates. In
L35@P1: this paper, we exploit high-frequency price changes within narrow windows around U.S. Treasury
L36@P1: auctions to measure the impact of unexpected shifts in investor demand for short- and longterm U.S. government securities on FX rates and government bond yields. As a novel fact we
L37@P1: document that the U.S. dollar systematically depreciates in response to unexpected demand shifts
L38@P1: for U.S. Treasuries. The effect is substantial in magnitude, persistent over time, and observable
L39@P1: across a broad cross-section of currencies, with spillovers extending into foreign bond markets. We
L40@P1: further show that whether unexpected shifts in demand for U.S. Treasuries mostly transmit to a
L41@P1: foreign country through changes in its exchange rate with the U.S. dollar or through changes in
L42@P1: its government bond yields depends on how correlated the country’s short-term interest rate is
L43@P1: with that of the U.S..
L44@P1: To establish this finding, we follow Ray et al. (2024) and posit that the institutional setup
L45@P1: of Treasury auctions offers a quasi-ideal environment to isolate and observe shifts in investor demand. These auctions are regular, pre-scheduled events, closely monitored by market participants
L46@P1: worldwide, where the supply of safe assets is fixed and publicly known in advance. Ray et al.
L47@P1: (2024) show that any observed fluctuations in U.S. Treasury prices around the time of the auction
L48@P1: reflect unexpected shifts in investor demand revealed at auction rather than information about
L49@P1: macro fundamentals.
L50@P1-2: 1To examine the impact of demand shifts on FX and global bond markets, we utilize granular,
L51@P2: high-frequency data on U.S. Treasury futures across various maturities and exchange rates for G9
L52@P2: currencies against the U.S. dollar over the period 2002–2018. Together, these currencies account
L53@P2: for nearly 70% of total daily global FX market turnover, reflecting the majority of global activity.
L54@P2: By focusing on these highly liquid and actively traded currency pairs, our analysis provides a
L55@P2: detailed view of how FX and bond markets jointly respond to shifts in demand for U.S. safe
L56@P2: assets. This approach also offers a unique opportunity to use both markets to empirically test the
L57@P2: predictions of segmented market models within a well-defined conceptual framework.
L58@P2: Our findings can be summarized as follows. First, by focusing on price changes of U.S. Treasury
L59@P2: futures within short windows around U.S. Treasury auctions, we document that in response to
L60@P2: unexpected demand shocks the U.S. dollar depreciates by approximately 2 basis points against a
L61@P2: broad cross-section of foreign currencies. This depreciation is highly statistically significant and
L62@P2: remains a robust feature of the data. We demonstrate that the U.S. dollar depreciation persists
L63@P2: across various measures of demand shocks and withstands a range of robustness tests. We extend
L64@P2: the analysis to global bond markets and find that global bond returns increase, on average, by
L65@P2: over 8 basis points. This provides evidence that demand shocks for U.S. safe assets spill over to
L66@P2: global fixed income markets.
L67@P2: Second, we demonstrate that the impact of demand shocks varies with the maturity of issued
L68@P2: Treasury instruments. For 2-year auctions, the U.S. dollar depreciates by only 0.70 basis points
L69@P2: (statistically insignificant), but this response increases consistently with maturity, reaching 3.66
L70@P2: basis points around 30-year Treasury auctions (significant at the 1% level). In bond markets, a
L71@P2: similar pattern emerges: the impact of increased Treasury demand rises from just over 1 basis
L72@P2: point for 2-year bonds to more than 37 basis points for 30-year bonds.
L73@P2: Having established the significant price impact of Treasury demand on currency and bond
L74@P2: markets, we address two key robustness concerns. First, we show that auction days are unique, as
L75@P2: there is no consistent relationship between Treasuries and these markets during the usual auction
L76@P2: times but evaluated on non-auction days. To verify this, we perform a block-bootstrap exercise
L77@P2: on non-auction days, constructing placebo demand shocks and repeating our baseline regressions.
L78@P2: Across 10,000 randomly drawn samples, we find average coefficients of -0.25 for FX and 2.34 for
L79@P2: bond markets, which are statistically distinct from the observed demand shock coefficients on
L80@P2: auction days.
L81@P2-3: 2We proceed assessing the persistence of demand shocks beyond the auctions. Using local projections, we find that foreign currency appreciation and bond market effects last for several days.
L82@P3: In panel regressions across currencies, U.S. dollar depreciation peaks at nearly 20 basis points
L83@P3: around day 10, gradually reverting to insignificance after 14 days. In bond markets, foreign bond
L84@P3: yields increase by over 8 basis points initially, remain elevated for about a week, and taper off
L85@P3: to insignificance after approximately 28 days. These results demonstrate strong and persistent
L86@P3: effects of demand shifts across both market segments. The prolonged impact highlights the interconnectedness of global financial markets, where shifts in U.S. safe asset demand trigger enduring
L87@P3: spillover effects in foreign bond yields and currencies as global investors presumably adjust their
L88@P3: portfolios.
L89@P3: Third, we identify a distinct cross-sectional pattern in how currencies and bonds respond to
L90@P3: Treasury demand shifts during auctions. While the U.S. dollar depreciates against all currencies,
L91@P3: the magnitude of depreciation varies. For example, the U.S. dollar weakens by only 0.55 and
L92@P3: 0.92 basis points against the CAD and AUD, respectively (not statistically significant), but shows
L93@P3: much larger declines of 2.20 and 3.43 basis points against the NOK and JPY. In bond markets,
L94@P3: this pattern is reversed: the demand impact ranges from 2.96 and 6.25 basis points for the JPY
L95@P3: and NOK to as high as 10.97 and 13.55 basis points for the CAD and GBP.
L96@P3: We attribute these variations to differences in short-rate correlations between the foreign country and the U.S. In the cross-section, currencies of countries with lower short-rate correlations to
L97@P3: the U.S. exhibit stronger depreciation, whereas bonds from these same countries show weaker yield
L98@P3: changes. Conversely, higher short-rate correlations are associated with smaller currency movements but larger bond yield responses. The correlation between short-rate correlations and FX
L99@P3: responses is strongly negative (-0.86), while the correlation with bond yield responses is strongly
L100@P3: positive (0.86). Using fixed-effects panel regressions, we confirm that the impact of Treasury demand shocks is systematically linked to short-rate correlations. The regression results show that
L101@P3: currencies and bonds respond in opposite directions, with the bond market impact increasing with
L102@P3: the maturity of the instrument.
L103@P3: Our findings align with the quantity-driven theory of risk premia (Gourinchas et al., 2024;
L104@P3: Greenwood et al., 2023). A positive demand shock for U.S. Treasuries lowers Treasury yields
L105@P3: and weakens the U.S. dollar. This occurs because global arbitrageurs, holding fewer Treasuries,
L106@P3: face reduced exposure to U.S. short-term interest rate risk, which lowers the term premium.
L107@P3-4: 3Simultaneously, their diminished interest rate risk also reduces the exchange rate risk premium,
L108@P4: causing the U.S. dollar to depreciate.
L109@P4: The strength of this negative relationship between U.S. Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar
L110@P4: weakens when U.S. and the foreign country’s short-term interest rates are highly correlated. A
L111@P4: higher correlation leads to a weaker response of the bilateral interest rate differential when the
L112@P4: U.S. short rate changes, thereby reducing the interest rate risk of foreign currency positions as the
L113@P4: uncovered interest parity (UIP) channel is mitigated. This dampens the co-movement between
L114@P4: Treasury yields and the exchange rate in response to Treasury demand shocks.
L115@P4: Finally, the positive co-movement between U.S. and foreign bond yields becomes stronger as the
L116@P4: correlation between their short-term interest rates increases. Greater alignment in short-term rates
L117@P4: brings the expectations components of both countries’ yields closer, synchronizing risk exposures.
L118@P4: This amplifies the co-movement between U.S. and foreign term premia following Treasury demand
L119@P4: shocks.
L120@P4: Having established our main findings, we extend our analysis to further explore the dynamics
L121@P4: of Treasury demand shocks. Using alternative measures, we proxy shifts in investor demand
L122@P4: with unexpected changes in the bid-to-cover ratio, distinguishing between bidder types. We find
L123@P4: that indirect bidders, such as foreign central banks and institutional investors, play a key role
L124@P4: in the pass-through to FX and global bond markets. Additionally, the FX market response is
L125@P4: amplified when a larger share of Treasuries is allocated to foreign investors and investment funds,
L126@P4: underscoring the role of U.S. Treasuries as safe-haven assets.
L127@P4: To further evaluate this mechanism, we replicate the stock-bond correlation measure of Hu
L128@P4: et al. (2024) and re-examine price impact regressions, distinguishing between auction days when
L129@P4: Treasuries are perceived as safe or risky assets. We find significant differences in market responses
L130@P4: depending on investor perceptions. On safe-asset days, foreign currencies, especially the AUD and
